Situation1: There is a scheduled family gathering on the calendar.
Expectation2: Ensure the safe and punctual operation of the subway train.
Situation2: A minor signal delay up ahead requires careful speed adjustments to maintain the schedule without causing abrupt movements.
Story: I glance at the family group chat on my phone during my break, seeing photos of my grandkids already gathered around the table, laughter frozen in pixels. Today was supposed to be our family gathering, a promise I made weeks ago. My daughter’s message—“Can’t wait to see you, Dad!”—echoes in my mind as I step back into the subway cab. But as I grip the controls, a warning light blinks: a minor signal delay ahead. Dispatch expects me to keep the train on schedule, adjusting speed with precision so passengers aren’t jolted. My supervisor’s words ring in my ears: “Safety and punctuality, always.” I feel the weight of two worlds—my family waiting for me, expecting stories and hugs, and the passengers behind me, trusting I’ll get them home safely and on time. My heart aches with the tug-of-war between the warmth of my family and the cold responsibility of the tracks. I stare at the tunnel ahead, torn, knowing I can’t be in two places at once.
